summary: Defines the basic components of a Network Standard Data Specification syntax, a mechanism for specifying all the attributes of a collection of bits. It replaces RFC 615.

plainLanguage.summary: The Network Standard Data Specification (NSDS) describes the location and attributes of a collection of bits. This RFC defines its basic syntax and pathname fields, with separate forms for people and computers.

questions: describing data format on the arpanet
what is the network standard data specification
subtitle: A common syntax for describing data attributes and file pathnames across hosts.

tldr.problem: Different hosts used different file naming conventions, making it hard to describe a collection of bits in a common way.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Standard Data Specification uses keyed pathname fields in a human-oriented or machine-oriented form.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the basic syntax and pathname fields, while leaving other data attributes for later work. It replaces RFC 615.

today: RFC 645 is listed with status Unknown and replaces RFC 615. The RFC says the complete NSDS syntax would require further work.

sections.title: Two Forms of NSDS
sections.content:
A Network Standard Data Specification (NSDS) is intended to specify attributes of a collection of bits. Because a complete syntax would take more work, RFC 645 defines a basic syntax and a complete pathname syntax.

The semi-structured form is intended for people: keywords can vary in length and data values use delimiters. The highly structured form is intended for computers: keywords have fixed length and variable-length data is preceded by a byte count.
sections.plainLanguage: NSDS has one form designed for people and another for programs. Both describe the same kinds of information using different formatting rules.

sections.title: Fields and Delimiters
sections.content:
An NSDS begins with one percent sign for semi-structured form or two for highly structured form, followed by fields and a space. Pathname fields come before other attributes.

In the machine form, each field has a four-character keyword, a one-byte binary count, and the data. In the human form, a variable-length keyword precedes data enclosed by delimiters. Pathname fields follow a defined order, though defaulted fields may be omitted.
sections.plainLanguage: The opening percent sign tells a reader which form follows. Each field has a label and a value, with the value length counted for computers or enclosed by delimiters for people.

sections.title: Pathname Fields and Defaults
sections.content:
Pathname keys cover NETWORK, HOST, PERIPHERAL, VOLUME ID, DIRECTORY, FILE, TYPE, VERSION, and SITEPARM. The order starts with network and host and proceeds to device and file details.

SITEPARM can carry information specific to the host, such as an access specification or account number. The RFC offers guidelines for defaults, including ARPA for the network, the interpreting host for HOST, and the user's working directory for DIRECTORY.
sections.plainLanguage: A pathname can identify a network, host, device, directory, and file. A site-specific field can carry information that the general syntax does not define.

sections.title: Sample Pathnames
sections.content:
The RFC gives the same pathname in semi-structured and highly structured forms. One example identifies a message file at ISI; another uses repeated DIRECTORY fields to describe nested directories.

The examples show that delimiters and byte counts can represent the same pathname information. The RFC notes that the syntax is meant to be extensible, even when part of it does not suit a particular host.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how the two forms encode pathname fields. Repeated directory fields can describe a path with several directory levels.

references.text: Proposed Network Standard Data Pathname Syntax, RFC 615.
